title: The Milkmaid's Secret: Edward Jenner
summary: In the English countryside, people said that milkmaids who caught a mild illness from cows called cowpox never got smallpox. A farmer named Benjamin Jesty tried it on his family, and later a doctor named Edward Jenner tested the idea carefully on a boy called James Phipps. Jenner wrote it all down in a little book, and the word 'vaccine' was born from the Latin word for cow!

sections.heading: 'I Shall Never Have Smallpox'
paragraphs: Imagine walking down a muddy lane in Gloucestershire, in the west of England, in the 1770s. Hedges line the fields, church bells ring across the valley, and in every farmyard someone is milking cows by hand, twice a day, every day. Milking was skilled work, and it was very often done by young women and girls called milkmaids or dairymaids. They sat on low stools, pressed their cheeks against the warm flank of the cow, and squeezed the udder with their bare hands.

Sometimes the cows had sores on their udders and teats. This was a disease called cowpox. It made the cow uncomfortable, and it could spread to the hands of the person milking her. A milkmaid who caught cowpox might get a few painful blisters on her fingers or wrists, swollen glands under her arm and a mild fever for a few days. Then she got better. Cowpox was a nuisance, not a killer.

Here is the strange part. Country people had noticed, for a long time, that milkmaids who had once caught cowpox did not seem to catch smallpox, even when it swept through the village. In an age when smallpox killed many of the people it infected and scarred many survivors, that was a remarkable thing to notice. The belief was common enough that one dairymaid is reported to have told a doctor, quite calmly, 'I shall never have smallpox for I have had cowpox.'

Today we know why this folk wisdom was partly right. Cowpox and smallpox are caused by two different viruses, but they are close cousins. Both belong to a family of viruses scientists call orthopoxviruses. They look similar enough to the immune system, the body's defence network, that fighting off one of them can leave the body ready to recognise the other. Nobody in the 1700s knew anything about viruses or immune systems. They only knew what they saw on farms: the cowpox girls stayed safe.

Modern scientists have found that cows are not really the natural home of cowpox at all. The virus mostly lives in wild rodents, especially voles, and only now and then jumps into cattle, cats or people. That helps explain something that puzzled people at the time: cowpox came and went. Some years a farm would have it, and some years it would vanish completely. As we will see, that made it very hard to study.

It is worth remembering what people already had to protect themselves. As you read in earlier parts, variolation, giving a healthy person material from a real smallpox sore, had been used for centuries in Asia and Africa and had spread through Britain since the 1720s. It worked, but it was dangerous: about one or two in every hundred variolated people died, and while they were sick they could pass real smallpox to others. If a gentle cow disease could do the same job, it would be a gift. A few bold people decided to find out.

sections.heading: The Farmer with a Darning Needle
paragraphs: The first person we know of who deliberately used cowpox to protect his family was not a famous doctor. He was a farmer named Benjamin Jesty, born in the village of Yetminster in Dorset, in the south-west of England, and baptised there in August 1736. His father was a butcher. In 1770 Benjamin married Elizabeth Notley, and together they would have seven children.

Jesty had caught cowpox himself when he was younger, and so had two of the servants who worked on his farm. He had noticed that these servants could nurse people sick with smallpox without catching it. In 1774 smallpox broke out in the Yetminster area. Jesty was frightened for his wife and his two eldest sons, Robert and Benjamin. He knew of a farm at nearby Chetnole where the cows had cowpox.

So he made a decision that shocked his neighbours. He took Elizabeth and the two boys to the cows at Chetnole, and using a darning needle, a large sewing needle for mending socks, he scratched material from the cows' sores into their arms. The boys had only mild reactions. Elizabeth's arm became badly swollen and inflamed, and for a while the family worried, but she recovered.

Many local people were horrified. Putting a disease from an animal into a human body seemed unnatural and even wicked. According to later accounts, Jesty was called inhuman and was jeered at and pelted when he went to local markets. But the experiment seemed to work. In later years, when his sons were exposed to smallpox, they did not catch it.

Jesty did not write a book or send a report to any scientific society. He was a farmer, not a scientist, and his test involved only his own family. For more than twenty years, almost nobody outside Dorset knew about it. Around 1797 he moved his family to Downshay Manor Farm at Worth Matravers, near the Dorset coast.

His story was not completely forgotten. In 1805, after vaccination had become famous, a London group called the Original Vaccine Pock Institution invited Jesty to the city. Twelve medical men questioned him about what he had done. To show the protection had lasted, his eldest son Robert, then 28, agreed to be inoculated with smallpox material again, and once more he did not become ill. The Institution gave Jesty a written testimonial and a pair of gold-mounted lancets, small surgical knives, as a reward. An artist, Michael William Sharp, painted his portrait, which is now owned by the Wellcome Trust and has been shown at the Dorset Museum.

Jesty was not alone, either. In 1791 a teacher named Peter Plett, in what is now northern Germany, also tried giving people cowpox to protect them. Folk ideas about cowpox seem to have been known in several parts of Europe. Jesty died in April 1816, and his gravestone at Worth Matravers still says that he was the first known person to introduce cowpox by inoculation. So why do most people today remember a different name? To answer that, we need to meet a country doctor from Gloucestershire.

sections.heading: A Curious Country Doctor
paragraphs: Edward Jenner was born on 17 May 1749 in Berkeley, a small market town in Gloucestershire near the River Severn. He was the eighth of nine children. His father, the Reverend Stephen Jenner, was the vicar of Berkeley, and Edward grew up surrounded by books, fields, birds and farm animals.

When Edward was a schoolboy, he was variolated against smallpox, along with many other children of families who could afford it. He went through the whole process: the preparation, the deliberate infection and the illness that followed. He survived, but the experience stayed with him. Some historians believe that remembering how unpleasant and risky variolation was helped make him interested in finding something safer.

At the age of 13 he was apprenticed for seven years to Daniel Ludlow, a surgeon in the nearby town of Chipping Sodbury. An apprentice learned by doing: mixing medicines, dressing wounds, helping with operations and watching the patients. It was during this time, according to the story Jenner and his friends told later, that he heard a dairymaid boast that she could never catch smallpox because she had already had cowpox. Some historians doubt the story happened exactly like that, but one way or another the idea lodged in his mind.

In 1770, aged 21, Jenner went to London to study surgery and anatomy at St George's Hospital under John Hunter, one of the most famous surgeons and experimenters of the age. Hunter collected thousands of specimens and was always testing ideas. He passed on to Jenner a famous piece of advice that came from the physician William Harvey: 'Don't think; try.' Hunter meant that you should not just argue about an idea, you should do an experiment and see. Jenner and Hunter stayed friends and wrote letters to each other for years.

By 1773 Jenner was back in Berkeley, working as a family doctor and surgeon. He visited patients on horseback, often riding long distances along country lanes. He also played music, wrote poems and loved natural history. One of his great projects was a study of the cuckoo. People believed the adult cuckoo threw the other birds' eggs out of the nest where it had laid its own egg. Jenner watched carefully and showed that it was actually the newly hatched cuckoo chick that pushed out the eggs and chicks, using a little hollow in its back to lift them. His paper was published in 1788, and the same year he was elected a Fellow of the Royal Society, Britain's leading scientific club.

Not everyone believed his cuckoo observation. For more than a hundred years, some of his critics pointed to it as proof that Jenner was careless. Then, in the early 1920s, photographs and a film of a cuckoo chick showed he had been right all along. That tells us something about Jenner: he was patient, he watched closely, and he was willing to say things other people did not believe.

In 1788 he married Catherine Kingscote, and they had three children: Edward, Catherine and Robert. Through all these years, the cowpox question kept coming back to him. He collected stories from farmers and dairy workers and noted cases of people who had had cowpox and then failed to catch smallpox when variolated. But stories are not proof. To really know, he would need to test it.

sections.heading: Sarah, Blossom and James: 14 May 1796
paragraphs: Cowpox was unpredictable. For years it did not appear on the farms near Berkeley in the right way for Jenner to use it. Then, in the spring of 1796, it did. A young dairymaid named Sarah Nelmes caught cowpox while milking a cow. The cow had a name: Blossom. Sarah had fresh cowpox blisters on her hand, full of clear fluid.

Jenner now needed someone who had never had smallpox or cowpox, so that he could see clearly whether cowpox protected them. He chose James Phipps, the eight-year-old son of his gardener. It is important to say plainly that we do not know how much James or his parents understood about what was going on, and James was far too young to agree for himself. In the 1790s, doctors did not have rules about consent like we have today, and many experiments were done on children, servants and poor people who had little power to say no.

On 14 May 1796, Jenner took a lancet, a small, sharp surgical blade, and scraped some fluid from the sores on Sarah's hand. Then he made two small, shallow cuts on James's arm, each only about as long as a fingernail, and placed the cowpox material into them. That was all. It took a few minutes.

Over the next days, Jenner watched the boy closely and wrote down what happened. A small sore formed where the material had gone in, much like the ones on Sarah's hand. On about the seventh day James complained of discomfort in his armpit, where the glands had swollen. On the ninth day he felt chilly, lost his appetite and had a slight headache. He spent one restless night. The next day he was well again. The sore on his arm slowly healed, leaving a small scar.

Think about how different that was from variolation. A variolated child might be ill for a couple of weeks, covered in smallpox spots, and could pass real smallpox to everyone around them. James had a sore arm and one bad night. But Jenner still had not proved anything. A mild cowpox infection was only useful if it really protected against smallpox. And the only way people in 1796 knew to check for protection was a frightening one.

Blossom, by the way, became one of the most famous cows in history. Her horns now hang in Jenner's old house in Berkeley, which is a museum called Dr Jenner's House, and her hide is kept in the library of St George's, University of London, the medical school linked to the hospital where Jenner trained.

sections.heading: The Test That Would Never Be Allowed Today
paragraphs: On 1 July 1796, about seven weeks after the cowpox, Jenner did what doctors of his time did to check whether a person was already immune to smallpox. He variolated James. He took material from a real smallpox sore and put it into small cuts in the boy's arm, exactly as he would have done to any patient being inoculated in the normal way.

If James had not been protected, he would very likely have developed variolated smallpox, the same illness that Jenner himself had gone through as a boy, with its fever, spots and small risk of death. Instead, nothing much happened. A little redness appeared where the cuts were made, and then faded. James did not get sick. Months later, Jenner tested him again with smallpox material, and again there was no illness.

We need to be very clear about this: an experiment like this would never be allowed today. Deliberately exposing a child to a deadly disease to see what happens breaks the basic rules of modern medical ethics. Today, every test of a new medicine or vaccine must be checked in advance by an independent ethics committee. Volunteers, or for children their parents and the child too where possible, must be told about the risks and agree freely. The whole system of clinical trials you will meet later in this story was built partly because of past experiments in which people, often the poorest or least powerful, were put at risk without proper protection.

To be fair to Jenner, he was working inside the rules of his own time. Variolating someone was normal, everyday medicine in 1796, and thousands of parents chose it for their own children. Jenner was not inventing a new danger; he was using the standard test of the day. But we can admire his curiosity and still say that the way he tested his idea on a child would be wrong now.

James Phipps grew up, married and had a family, and he lived until 1853. He was variolated many more times during his life, twenty or more according to some accounts, and is said never to have caught smallpox. When Jenner later wrote up his research, James appeared as Case 17 in the list of patients.

sections.heading: The Little Book That Named Vaccines
paragraphs: One boy is not enough to prove anything. James might have been naturally resistant, or the smallpox material might have been weak. Jenner knew this. In 1797 he wrote a short report about his findings and sent it to the Royal Society. The Society did not publish it. The evidence, the reviewers felt, was too thin.

Jenner wanted more cases, but he faced a frustrating problem: cowpox had disappeared from the local farms. He had to wait. Only in the spring of 1798 did it come back. Now he worked quickly. He gave cowpox to more children, including his own baby son Robert, who was 11 months old. He also tried something important: taking material from the sore of one vaccinated child and putting it into the arm of the next child, to see whether cowpox could be passed on from person to person without a cow. It could. That discovery would turn out to be hugely important, as you will see in the next part.

In 1798 Jenner published, at his own expense, a short book with a very long title: 'An Inquiry into the Causes and Effects of the Variolae Vaccinae, a Disease Discovered in Some of the Western Counties of England, Particularly Gloucestershire, and Known by the Name of the Cow Pox.' It described 23 cases, including people who had caught cowpox naturally years before and then resisted variolation, and the children he had given it to on purpose. It included beautiful coloured pictures of cowpox sores, including the sores on Sarah Nelmes's hand.

'Variolae vaccinae' was Jenner's Latin name for cowpox. It means something like 'smallpox of the cow'. 'Variola' was the name for smallpox, and 'vacca' is Latin for cow. From this came the words 'vaccine' for the cowpox material and 'vaccination' for the process of giving it. Much later, the French scientist Louis Pasteur suggested using the word vaccine for all preparations like this, as a tribute to Jenner. So every time someone says the word vaccine today, they are, without realising it, talking about cows.

The Inquiry was not perfect. Jenner got some things wrong. He suggested that cowpox started in horses, coming from a horse disease called 'the grease' which was carried to cows on the hands of farm workers who looked after both animals. Most experts rejected that idea. He also believed at first that one vaccination would protect a person for their entire life; later experience showed that protection could fade over many years. And 23 cases was a small number by any standard. But the central idea was right, and it was written down clearly enough that other doctors could test it for themselves.

sections.heading: Safer, Kinder, and Not Contagious
paragraphs: Why did Jenner's idea matter so much, if variolation already existed? The answer is safety. Variolation used real smallpox virus. Even though the illness was usually milder than catching smallpox naturally, about one or two of every hundred variolated people died. Worse, a variolated person was infectious. They could start a real smallpox outbreak in their town, which is why they had to be kept away from other people for weeks.

Vaccination with cowpox was far safer. Serious problems were rare. The person usually had just a sore at the spot and maybe a day or two of feeling unwell. Most important of all, a vaccinated person could not spread smallpox to anyone, because there was no smallpox in them at all. They could go to school, go to work and see their families. That made it possible, for the first time, to imagine protecting whole cities and countries without risk of starting epidemics.

At first it was slow going. When Jenner went to London to find volunteers, he spent about three months without persuading anyone. Then other doctors took up the work, including the surgeon Henry Cline and the physicians George Pearson and William Woodville. They tested vaccination on many more people. Not everything went smoothly: some early London vaccine got mixed with smallpox material in a hospital that treated both, causing confusion. But the results kept coming in, and they were good.

Jenner spent much of the rest of his life promoting vaccination, answering letters from all over the world and sending vaccine to doctors who asked for it, usually for free. In the garden of his house in Berkeley he had a small, rustic summer house that he called the Temple of Vaccinia. There, according to local tradition, he vaccinated poor local people free of charge. It has been called the world's first vaccination clinic, and you can still visit it.

The British Parliament rewarded him with £10,000 in 1802 and another £20,000 in 1807, after the Royal College of Physicians confirmed that vaccination worked. Those were huge sums at the time. Even Napoleon, whose France was at war with Britain, had his soldiers vaccinated and gave Jenner a medal. When Jenner asked him to release some English prisoners, Napoleon is reported to have said that he could not refuse anything to one of the greatest benefactors of mankind. Jenner died in Berkeley on 26 January 1823, aged 73, and is buried in the church of St Mary there, close to the house where he did his work.

sections.heading: Who Gets the Credit?
paragraphs: So who invented vaccination? The honest answer is that it was not one person. Many people, probably over many years and in several countries, noticed that cowpox seemed to protect against smallpox. That idea belonged to milkmaids and farmers before it belonged to any doctor. Benjamin Jesty used cowpox on purpose about 22 years before Jenner's experiment with James Phipps, and Peter Plett tried it in 1791. And long before any of them, healers in China, India, Africa and the Ottoman Empire had worked out that a deliberate, controlled infection could protect against smallpox. Jenner was not the first person to protect anyone against smallpox, and he did not invent the idea of using cowpox.

What Jenner did was different, and still very important. He tested the idea in a careful, organised way, writing down what happened to each person. He showed that cowpox could be passed from person to person, which meant the vaccine did not depend on finding a sick cow. He published his results so that anyone could read them, check them and argue about them. And then he spent the rest of his life spreading the method, sending vaccine around the world and arguing its case. The historian Donald Hopkins has pointed out that Jenner's key contribution was not the first use of cowpox, but showing that the people he vaccinated really were immune to smallpox.

Science works a lot like this. An idea often floats around for years before someone tests it carefully and shares it widely. Recognising Jesty, Plett and the unnamed milkmaids does not take anything away from Jenner. It just makes the story truer, and it reminds us that discoveries are usually built by many hands.

By 1800, Jenner's little book had been translated into other languages and vaccination was spreading across Europe and beyond. But there was a serious problem. The vaccine was alive. It had to be taken fresh from a sore and put into the next person within days, or it stopped working. There were no refrigerators, no aeroplanes and no way to keep a living virus safe on a voyage lasting months. So how could anyone possibly send a living vaccine across oceans to the other side of the world?

deepDive: Jenner's 1798 Inquiry is a fascinating document to read with modern eyes. Of its 23 cases, most were people who had caught cowpox naturally, sometimes decades earlier, and who then failed to develop smallpox when variolated or exposed. Only a handful were deliberate vaccinations, and the crucial evidence for protection rested on challenge by variolation, a method that is impossible to repeat today. By modern standards the study had no control group, tiny numbers and no blinding. What made it persuasive was the combination of a clear claim, a biological mechanism that others could reproduce, and Jenner's demonstration that cowpox could be passed arm to arm, freeing vaccination from the unpredictable appearance of cowpox on farms. Within a few years, thousands of vaccinations by other doctors provided the large-scale evidence that Jenner's own numbers could not. Why does cowpox protect against smallpox at all? Cowpox virus and variola virus are both orthopoxviruses, and they share many proteins with very similar shapes. Antibodies and immune cells trained against one can recognise the other, a phenomenon called cross-protection. That same family resemblance is why vaccines based on the related virus vaccinia were later used to eradicate smallpox. Historians still debate how to divide credit. Jesty's 1774 inoculation is well documented, and Jesty's gravestone calls him the first known person to introduce cowpox by inoculation. Others, such as Peter Plett in 1791, did similar things. Jenner's defenders argue that a discovery only becomes part of science when it is tested systematically and published, which Jenner did and the others did not. Critics point out that Jenner received £30,000 from Parliament while Jesty received nothing, and that Jenner made mistakes, such as his theory that cowpox came from the horse disease called grease and his early belief that one vaccination gave lifelong protection. Interestingly, the horse idea is not as silly as it once seemed: as the next part explains, genetic studies suggest the vaccine virus used later is closely related to horsepox. A fair conclusion is that vaccination grew from folk knowledge, the bravery and stubbornness of individuals like Jesty, and Jenner's careful work and tireless promotion, which turned a rural belief into a method used around the world.
funFact: The horns of Blossom, the cow whose cowpox started Jenner's famous 1796 experiment, are still kept at Jenner's house museum in Berkeley, and her hide is kept at St George's medical school in London.
